new_statements.quote: Primary stress is generally on the penultimate syllable, but can fall on long vowels or diphthongs that occur in the final or antepenultimate position. Vowel lengthening also indicates pragmatic force or semantic alternations, such as lengthening to indicate a longer duration of an event. Intonation phrasing tends to have a contrastive phrase-final accent — i.e. the final segment of the phrase is where intonation contrast is distinguished.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default penultimate stress; a long vowel or diphthong (a heavy syllable) in the final or antepenultimate syllable attracts primary stress away from the penult. So: stress the heavy syllable within the last three syllables if there is one, otherwise the penult. Vowel length is contrastive (long vowels written as geminates, p. 22).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by Hammond 2015. Lynch 2001 (PL 509, p. 9), speaking of the Tanna languages as a group, says secondary stress normally falls two syllables to the left of the primary-stressed syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: None beyond the long-vowel/diphthong attraction; the author hedges with 'generally'. Vowel lengthening can also be pragmatic/semantic (duration of event), which may interact with stress placement.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement in a grammar-sketch chapter (phonology outline in a syntax dissertation), not an instrumental study. Phrase-level: intonation phrases carry a contrastive phrase-final accent, explicitly distinguished from word stress. Data are from the Yenamakel village dialect (Hammond 2009: 9 n. 2).
new_statements.identity_note: Hammond's Whitesands data (2009, 2015) come from the dialect of Yenamakel (Ienamakel) village on the east coast of Tanna; no separate Glottolog dialect code known — treat as whit1269. Gray 1891 calls the same variety 'Weasisi'. Lynch 2001's statement is at the level of 'the Tanna languages' (whit1269, lena1238, nort2867, sout2869, kwam1252) collectively.

sources.locator: Chapter 2 'Phonology and word classes', sec. 2.1.3 'Phonotactics and stress', p. 23 (PDF page 39)
sources.note: Sec. 2.1.3 'Phonotactics and stress', p. 23: primary stress generally penultimate, but falls on long vowels or diphthongs in final or antepenultimate position; vowel lengthening also pragmatic/semantic; intonation phrases carry a contrastive phrase-final accent. Also p. 22: schwa is an allophone of other low vowels in unstressed positions. Nothing on secondary stress.

sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: open copy online
sources.note: Ch. 3 orthography only; one passing remark p. 24 that Lenakel/Whitesands orthographies 'are based on the assumption that [a] becomes [ə] when unstressed'. No stress-placement rule for any Tanna language.

sources.citation: Lynch, John. 2001. The Linguistic History of Southern Vanuatu. Pacific Linguistics 509. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Sec. 1.5.2 p. 9 (family-level, covering 'the Tanna languages' collectively, Whitesands included): 'In Anejom and the Tanna languages, it is normally penultimate, but (a) final if the vowel of the final syllable is long, and (b) antepenultimate in certain very restricted contexts. Secondary stress normally occurs two syllables to the left of the primary-stressed syllable.' Sec. 4.4.3 p. 117: all daughter languages have regular penultimate stress; long vowels in final syllables attract stress.
